name: Backend developer
summary: Backend developer interviews usually focus on APIs, databases and how a service behaves under load or failure, alongside coding in the role's main language (often Java, Python, Node.js, Go or C#). Candidates commonly report questions on SQL and indexing, caching, concurrency and authentication, and for experienced roles, a system design round and stories about production incidents.
rounds: Online coding test or take-home: often a coding problem or a small API to build
Coding interview in the role's main language
Backend fundamentals: databases, APIs, caching, concurrency and your framework
System design for experienced roles: design a service and discuss scale and failure
looks_for: Clean API design: resources, status codes, versioning and errors
Database judgement: schema design, indexes, transactions and query cost
Knowing what happens under load: caching, queues, timeouts and retries
Security basics: authentication, authorisation and validating input
Debugging from logs and metrics, and owning production issues
Real depth in one language and framework

questions.text: Tell me about a production incident you were part of. What was your role in fixing it?
covers: What users saw and how the team found out
What you checked and how you narrowed down the cause
The fix and the follow-up: alerts, tests or design changes

questions.text: Describe a time you sped up a slow API or query. How did you find the problem?
covers: How slow it was and who it affected
How you found the cause: query plans, profiling, tracing
What you changed, with before-and-after numbers

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to change a database schema or API that other teams depended on.
covers: Why the change was needed
How you kept things working during the change: versioning, backward compatibility, migrating in steps
How you told the other teams, and what you'd do differently

questions.text: Tell me about a technical shortcut you took to meet a deadline. Did you go back and fix it?
covers: The shortcut and why it seemed worth it at the time
What it cost later, honestly
How you paid it back, or how you'd decide differently now

questions.text: What makes a REST API well designed? Talk me through one you've built.
covers: Clear resource names, the right HTTP methods and status codes
Consistent error responses, pagination and versioning
Authentication, rate limits and documentation

questions.text: Explain database indexes. How do they speed up reads, and what do they cost?
covers: An index as a sorted structure (often a B-tree) that avoids scanning every row
Composite indexes and why column order matters
The cost on writes and storage, and checking a query plan to confirm an index is used

questions.text: What are transactions and ACID, and when might you accept a weaker isolation level?
covers: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability in plain words
Problems isolation prevents, such as dirty reads and lost updates
The trade-off between strict isolation and throughput, with an example

questions.text: When would you choose a relational database, and when a NoSQL store?
covers: Relational for structured data, joins and strong consistency
Document, key-value or wide-column stores for flexible shapes or very high write rates
Letting the access patterns decide, with an example from your work

questions.text: How would you add caching to a read-heavy service, and how do you stop it serving stale data?
covers: What to cache and where: in memory, a shared cache such as Redis, a CDN
Expiry times, clearing entries on writes, and cache-aside versus write-through
What happens if the cache goes down or many requests miss at once

questions.text: Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation, and how token-based login works.
covers: Who you are versus what you're allowed to do
Issuing a signed token, sending it with each request and verifying it on the server
Expiry and refresh tokens, and storing passwords with a slow, salted hash

questions.text: Your service calls a payment provider that sometimes times out. How do you make this safe?
covers: Timeouts, and retries with backoff rather than retrying blindly
Idempotency keys so a retry can't charge the customer twice
Recording each payment's state and reconciling uncertain ones later

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd design a notification service that sends email, SMS and push messages.
covers: Requirements: volume, priority, user preferences and quiet hours
A queue between the API and the senders, with retries and a dead-letter queue
Rate limits per provider, avoiding duplicates, and tracking delivery

questions.text: Two requests update the same record at the same moment and one change is lost. Why, and how would you prevent it?
covers: The read-modify-write race and why it happens
Fixes: row locks, optimistic locking with a version number, single atomic updates
How you'd reproduce it in a test

questions.text: When would you put a message queue between two services instead of a direct API call?
covers: Moving slow or unreliable work out of the user's request
Absorbing spikes and retrying failures
The costs: delayed consistency, duplicate messages, harder debugging

questions.text: Explain how your main framework handles a request, from reaching the server to sending the response.
covers: Routing, middleware, the handler and the response
Where validation, authentication and error handling sit
How it serves many requests at once: threads, an event loop or worker processes

questions.text: Why backend development rather than frontend or full-stack work?
covers: What you enjoy: data, reliability, scale, the logic behind the product
An example from your work or projects that shows it
What you'd like to learn next

questions.text: What would you want to know about our systems and team before your first week?
covers: Questions about the stack, on-call, and how code is reviewed and shipped
A question that shows you've looked at the product
What a good first three months looks like to them

tips: Know your main language deeply: its concurrency model, how memory is managed, and the usual libraries for web work.
In any design question, ask about traffic, data size and how stale data is allowed to be before drawing boxes.
Bring up failure without being asked: timeouts, retries, duplicates and what happens when a dependency is down.
Practise reading a query plan and explaining why an index is or isn't being used.
Have one incident story ready with a timeline, your part in it and what changed afterwards.
